Comparison Table | Right | Protects against | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Safety | Hazardous goods | ISI mark | | Information | Misleading details | MRP, expiry date | | Choice | Monopoly, forced bundling | Many brands available | | Heard | Ignored complaints | Consumer helplines | | Redressal | Exploitation | Consumer Commission | | Education | Ignorance | Jago Grahak Jago | Memory aid: "SICHRE" – Safety, Information, Choice, Heard, Redressal, Education ("Stay Informed, Choose, Hear, Redress, Educate").

modules.title: Additional answers for syllabus depth
modules.body: These expand topics that were too brief in the condensed set. Existing question numbers are unchanged.

questions.title: Q33. What are cross-cultural influences? Why is cross-cultural understanding important?
questions.body: Introduction When companies sell in many countries or regions, they meet consumers with different languages, values and habits. Cross-cultural consumer analysis is the study of similarities and differences between consumers of different cultures or countries, to decide whether to use a standardised or a localised marketing strategy. 1. Areas of Cross-Cultural Difference 1. Language and meanings of words. 2. Values and religion. 3. Food habits. 4. Colours, symbols and gestures. 5. Gift customs and time orientation. 6. Family roles. 7. Level of income and technology. 2. Strategies for Cross-Cultural Marketing 1. Standardisation (global strategy): the same product and message worldwide. Example: Apple iPhone, Coca-Cola logo. 2. Localisation (adaptation): product and message adapted to local culture. Example: McDonald's McAloo Tikki, KFC's vegetarian menu in India. 3. Glocalisation: "think global, act local" – a global brand with local flavours and languages. 3. Importance of Cross-Cultural Understanding 1. Avoids cultural blunders such as wrong translations or offensive symbols. 2. Helps design acceptable products and packaging. 3. Improves communication effectiveness. 4. Builds trust and acceptance in new markets. Advantages of standardisation: lower cost and a consistent global image. Limitations of standardisation: may ignore local needs and cause rejection. Comparison Table | Basis | Standardisation | Localisation | Glocalisation | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Approach | Same everywhere | Adapted to each market | Global core, local touches | | Cost | Low | High | Medium | | Fit with local culture | Low | High | High | | Example | iPhone | McAloo Tikki | Domino's paneer pizzas | Example: A brand name that sounds fine in English may have a negative meaning in another language, so firms test names locally before launch.

questions.title: Q34. Explain the family life cycle and its marketing implications.
questions.body: Introduction A family's needs change as members marry, have children, grow older and retire. The Family Life Cycle (FLC) describes the stages a family passes through over time; each stage has different needs, income and buying patterns. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Bachelor"] --> B["Newly married"] --> C["Full nest I"] --> D["Full nest II"] --> E["Full nest III"] E --> F["Empty nest I"] --> G["Empty nest II"] --> H["Solitary survivor"] ``` Stages of the Family Life Cycle 1. Bachelor stage: young, single, living alone – fashion, gadgets, entertainment, travel. 2. Newly married couple: young, no children – furniture, appliances, holidays, home. 3. Full nest I: youngest child under 6 – baby food, toys, medicines, insurance. 4. Full nest II: youngest child 6 or older – education, tuition, bicycles, larger packs. 5. Full nest III: older couple with dependent grown-up children – higher education, second car, home upgrades. 6. Empty nest I: children have left home, head still working – travel, luxury items, investments. 7. Empty nest II: head retired, lower income – healthcare, pilgrimage, medical insurance. 8. Solitary survivor: one spouse alive – healthcare, care services, companionship. Modern variations: single parents, childless couples, divorced persons, live-in couples and people marrying later. Marketing Implications 1. Target products to each life stage. 2. Time offers to life events (weddings, childbirth, retirement). 3. Design life-stage insurance, banking and housing products. Comparison Table | Stage | Typical purchases | | --- | --- | | Bachelor | Fashion, gadgets | | Newly married | Furniture, appliances | | Full nest I | Baby products, insurance | | Full nest II | Education, larger packs | | Full nest III | Higher education, second car | | Empty nest I | Travel, luxury | | Empty nest II | Healthcare, pilgrimage | | Solitary survivor | Care services | Example: Banks offer education loans to Full nest II families and pension plans to Empty nest I couples.

questions.title: Q35. Explain Maslow's hierarchy and Alderfer's ERG theory, with consumer applications.
questions.body: Maslow's five levels: Physiological needs concern food and basic survival; safety concerns protection and stability; belonging concerns affection and social connection; esteem concerns respect and achievement; self-actualisation concerns developing one's potential. A product can serve several needs: a phone can support communication, belonging and status. Draw the five-level pyramid shown in Q12. Limits: Needs may coexist, and culture and circumstances affect their importance. Do not assume every consumer follows an identical fixed sequence. Introduction Clayton Alderfer (1969) revised Maslow's theory to make it more flexible and closer to research evidence. He condensed Maslow's five needs into three groups – Existence, Relatedness and Growth (ERG). 1. The Three Needs 1. Existence needs (E): material and physiological needs (= Maslow's physiological + safety). 2. Relatedness needs (R): relationships with others (= social + external esteem). 3. Growth needs (G): personal development (= internal esteem + self-actualisation). ```mermaid flowchart LR M5["Self-actualisation"] --> G["GROWTH"] M4a["Esteem (internal)"] --> G M4b["Esteem (external)"] --> R["RELATEDNESS"] M3["Social"] --> R M2["Safety"] --> X["EXISTENCE"] M1["Physiological"] --> X ``` 2. Key Ideas of ERG Theory 1. More than one need can operate at the same time. 2. No rigid order of needs. 3. Satisfaction–progression: a satisfied need leads to the next one. 4. Frustration–regression: if a higher need is frustrated, a person falls back to a lower need with more intensity (a person unable to grow in career spends more on material comforts). Comparison Table | Basis | Maslow | Alderfer (ERG) | | --- | --- | --- | | Number of needs | 5 | 3 | | Order | Usually presented as a hierarchy | Flexible; simultaneous needs | | Needs at a time | One dominant need | Several together | | Movement | Satisfaction–progression only | Satisfaction–progression and frustration–regression | | Emphasis | Five need categories | Three categories and frustration–regression | Example: A young employee who cannot get a promotion (growth frustrated) may compensate by buying an expensive bike (existence).

questions.title: Q36. Explain Herzberg, McClelland and McGregor, and distinguish their applications.
questions.body: Introduction Frederick Herzberg (1959) studied what makes people satisfied or dissatisfied at work. He found that satisfaction and dissatisfaction are caused by two different sets of factors – hygiene factors and motivators. The same idea applies to how consumers judge products. 1. Hygiene Factors (Dissatisfiers / Maintenance Factors) Their absence causes dissatisfaction; their presence only prevents dissatisfaction. 1. Workplace: salary, job security, working conditions, company policy, supervision. 2. Consumer: warranty, basic quality, safety, on-time delivery. 2. Motivators (Satisfiers) Their presence causes satisfaction and motivation. 1. Workplace: achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth, the work itself. 2. Consumer: unique features, attractive design, delight factors, prestige. | Factor type | When absent | When present | | --- | --- | --- | | Hygiene factors | Dissatisfaction | No dissatisfaction (but not satisfaction) | | Motivators | No satisfaction (but not dissatisfaction) | Satisfaction | 3. Relevance to Consumer Behaviour 1. Marketers must first provide hygiene factors (reliability, after-sales service, safety) so consumers are not dissatisfied. 2. To create preference and loyalty, they must add motivators – innovative features, superior design, emotional benefits. Comparison Table | Basis | Hygiene factors | Motivators | | --- | --- | --- | | Effect when absent | Dissatisfaction | No satisfaction | | Effect when present | No dissatisfaction | Satisfaction | | Work examples | Salary, job security | Recognition, growth | | Car example | Airbags, service network | Panoramic sunroof, premium feel | Example: In a car, airbags and a good service network are hygiene factors; a panoramic sunroof and premium interiors are motivators. McClelland's acquired needs: Achievement is the desire to meet challenging standards and receive performance feedback; affiliation is the desire for belonging and harmonious relationships; power is the desire to influence others. Their relative importance differs across people and experiences. Marketing appeals can emphasise accomplishing goals, connecting with others or exercising influence, without assuming a purchase reveals a person's dominant motive. McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y: These are contrasting managerial assumptions about workers. X assumes work avoidance and a need for close direction; Y recognises that people can exercise self-direction, accept responsibility and be creative under suitable conditions. They are not scientifically established categories of shoppers. Use them to explain managerial attitudes, then label any consumer analogy as an analogy. Comparison: Herzberg distinguishes causes of workplace dissatisfaction and satisfaction; McClelland examines acquired needs; McGregor examines assumptions used in management. Herzberg's application to products is an extension of a workplace theory.

questions.title: Q37. Explain Vroom and the Porter–Lawler expectancy model with an example.
questions.body: Introduction Victor Vroom (1964) explained motivation as a rational calculation. A person is motivated when they believe effort will lead to performance, performance will lead to a reward, and the reward is valued. Formula: Motivation (Force) = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence ```mermaid flowchart LR E["EFFORT"] -- Expectancy --> P["PERFORMANCE"] -- Instrumentality --> R["REWARD"] -- Valence --> V["Value to the person"] ``` 1. Components 1. Expectancy (E): belief that effort will lead to performance (0 to 1). 2. Instrumentality (I): belief that performance will lead to the reward (0 to 1). 3. Valence (V): value or attractiveness of the reward to the person (−1 to +1). 4. Because motivation is a product, if any one factor is zero, motivation is zero. 2. Numerical Example Given: A consumer is considering a fitness programme. E = 0.7 (she believes she can follow it), I = 0.9 (she believes following it will reduce weight), V = 0.8 (she values weight loss highly). To find: Motivation (M). Formula: M = E × I × V Solution: M = 0.7 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.504 Answer: Motivation = 0.504. Interpretation: an illustrative motivation score, not a purchase probability. If she believed the programme would give no results (I = 0), motivation would be 0. 3. Consumer Relevance 1. Increase expectancy – "easy to use", simple instructions. 2. Increase instrumentality – guarantees, proof, testimonials, cashback. 3. Increase valence – attractive rewards and emotional benefits. Comparison Table | Component | Question in the consumer's mind | Marketer's tool | | --- | --- | --- | | Expectancy | "Can I do it?" | Easy-to-use claims, demos | | Instrumentality | "Will it give the result?" | Guarantees, testimonials | | Valence | "Do I want the result?" | Attractive benefits | Porter–Lawler model: The value of a reward and perceived effort–reward probability influence effort. Performance depends on effort together with abilities, traits and understanding of the role. Performance produces intrinsic rewards, such as achievement, and extrinsic rewards, such as a prize. Satisfaction depends on the rewards and whether they seem equitable; experience affects future expectations. Flow: reward value + perceived probability → effort → performance (also influenced by ability and role clarity) → intrinsic/extrinsic rewards → perceived fairness → satisfaction and feedback. Difference: Vroom explains the motivation to exert effort; Porter–Lawler links effort, performance, rewards and satisfaction. For a loyalty scheme, consumers must value the reward, understand how to earn it and receive a reward they perceive as fair.

questions.title: Q38. Explain Freud's theory of motivation and its use in consumer research.
questions.body:
Introduction Sigmund Freud believed that human behaviour is driven largely by unconscious motives – desires people are not aware of. Applied to marketing, this means consumers may not know the real reasons why they buy. 1. Structure of Personality 1. Id: primitive, unconscious urges seeking immediate pleasure (pleasure principle). 2. Superego: the internal moral conscience – social and family values. 3. Ego: the conscious controller that balances the id and superego realistically (reality principle). ```mermaid flowchart TD SE["SUPEREGO
'Don't overspend, it's wrong'"] --> EG["EGO
balances → 'Buy it on a sale'"] ID["ID
'I want that luxury watch now!'"] --> EG ``` 2. Motivation Research Ernest Dichter applied Freud's ideas to marketing using qualitative techniques to uncover hidden motives: 1. Depth interviews: long, unstructured one-to-one interviews. 2. Focus groups: group discussions. 3. Projective techniques: word association, sentence completion, picture interpretation (TAT), role playing. 3. Marketing Implications 1. Use of symbolic and emotional appeals. 2. Products seen as extensions of personality. 3. Luxury purchases explained as satisfying hidden status or pleasure motives. 4. Guilt-reduction messages ("you deserve it"). Advantages: - Reveals hidden reasons for buying. - Helps create emotional and symbolic advertising. Limitations: - Based on small samples. - Interpretation is subjective. - Hard to measure or test scientifically. Comparison Table | Part | Principle | Consumer voice | | --- | --- | --- | | Id | Pleasure | "I want it now!" | | Superego | Morality | "It's wasteful." | | Ego | Reality | "Buy it on sale." | Example: A chocolate ad says "Go on, treat yourself – you deserve it", satisfying the id while calming the superego.

questions.title: Q39. Explain self-concept, trait, humanistic and social-cognitive personality theories.
questions.body: Introduction Unlike Freudian theory, which is qualitative, trait theory is a quantitative approach. It describes personality in terms of measurable traits – distinguishing, relatively enduring ways in which one person differs from another (such as sociable, confident or anxious). 1. Main Trait Theorists 1. Gordon Allport: cardinal, central and secondary traits. 2. Raymond Cattell: 16 personality factors (16PF), measured by questionnaire. 3. Big Five (OCEAN) model: five broad traits that describe most personalities. 2. The Big Five (OCEAN) Traits 1. Openness: curious, creative – tries new products, travel, gadgets. 2. Conscientiousness: organised, careful – compares carefully, values reliability. 3. Extraversion: sociable, outgoing – enjoys social events, fashion, group activities. 4. Agreeableness: friendly, cooperative – influenced by others' opinions. 5. Neuroticism: anxious, emotionally unstable – seeks reassurance, comfort and safety products. 3. Consumer-Specific Traits 1. Consumer innovativeness: willingness to try new products. 2. Dogmatism: rigidity towards unfamiliar ideas. 3. Social character: inner-directed vs other-directed. 4. Need for uniqueness and variety-seeking. 5. Optimum stimulation level and need for cognition. 6. Materialism and compulsive buying. 7. Consumer ethnocentrism: preference for domestic products ("Vocal for Local"). Advantages: - Measurable with questionnaires. - Useful for market segmentation. Limitations: - Traits alone poorly predict specific brand choice. - The situation also influences behaviour. Comparison Table | Trait | High scorers are | Consumer example | | --- | --- | --- | | Openness | Curious, creative | Try new gadgets | | Conscientiousness | Organised, careful | Read reviews, value reliability | | Extraversion | Sociable | Fashion, group activities | | Agreeableness | Cooperative | Follow friends' advice | | Neuroticism | Anxious | Buy safety and comfort products | Example: Consumers high in openness are the first to buy new tech such as foldable phones. Memory aid: OCEAN. Self-concept: Actual self is how someone sees themselves; ideal self is how they would like to be; social self is how they believe others see them; ideal social self is how they would like others to see them. Products may express or support these identities. For example, buying running shoes may support an aspiration to be more active; it does not prove the buyer already has that lifestyle. Humanistic theory: Maslow and Rogers emphasise growth, choice and personal potential. Rogers discusses self-concept and congruence between self and experience. Consumer applications include services that support learning and personal development, rather than assuming material purchases automatically produce fulfilment. Social-cognitive theory: Personal beliefs, behaviour and environment influence one another (reciprocal determinism). People learn from models and from consequences; self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to perform a specific task. Product demonstrations can build confidence. Unlike a trait-only explanation, this approach emphasises both the person and the situation. Comparison: Self-concept asks how buying relates to identity; trait theory measures individual differences; humanistic theory emphasises development; social-cognitive theory examines interaction and learning. Psychoanalytic and Neo-Freudian approaches remain in Q14.

questions.title: Q40. Explain operant, associative, trial-and-error and social learning with examples.
questions.body:
Introduction Operant conditioning, developed by B. F. Skinner, is learning based on the consequences of behaviour. Behaviour that is rewarded (reinforced) is likely to be repeated; behaviour that is punished or not rewarded is less likely. The consumer learns by trial and error which behaviours give the best results. Skinner box experiment: a rat that pressed a lever received food, so it learned to press the lever more often. ```mermaid flowchart LR B["Behaviour
(buy brand)"] --> C["Consequence"] --> R{"Reinforced?"} R -- Yes --> Y["Repeat purchase"] R -- No --> N["Stop buying"] ``` 1. Types of Reinforcement 1. Positive reinforcement: a pleasant reward after behaviour – the product works well; cashback, loyalty points. 2. Negative reinforcement: removing an unpleasant state – a painkiller removes a headache; insurance removes fear. 3. Punishment: an unpleasant result reduces behaviour – late payment fees. 4. Extinction: behaviour fades when the reward stops – a customer leaves when satisfaction ends. 2. Schedules of Reinforcement 1. Total (continuous): every purchase is rewarded (free gift every time). 2. Systematic (fixed ratio): every nth purchase is rewarded ("buy 9 coffees, get the 10th free"). 3. Random (variable ratio): rewards given at random (lucky draws, scratch cards). 3. Other Applications 1. Shaping: rewarding small steps towards the desired behaviour (free test drive → showroom visit → purchase). 2. Massed vs distributed learning: a concentrated ad burst gives quick learning (product launch); spread-out ads give longer-lasting learning. Comparison Table (Classical vs Operant) | Basis | Classical conditioning | Operant conditioning | | --- | --- | --- | | Proposed by | Pavlov | Skinner | | Learning through | Association of stimuli | Consequences (rewards / punishment) | | Response | Involuntary (automatic) | Voluntary | | Consumer role | Passive | Active | | Example | Jingle linked with brand | Cashback after purchase | Example: A coffee chain's app gives a free coffee after every nine purchases, encouraging customers to keep coming back (fixed-ratio positive reinforcement). Associative and trial-and-error learning: Consumers learn links between cues and outcomes and retain these in memory. In trial-and-error learning, they try alternatives and adjust later choices according to consequences. Thorndike's law of effect explains why a response followed by a satisfying result tends to be strengthened. A successful trial pack can encourage repurchase, but a poor experience can discourage it. Social/observational learning: Attention to a model → retention of the demonstrated behaviour → ability to reproduce it → motivation to do so. A customer can learn to use an appliance by watching a demonstration without first receiving a direct reward. Credible, relatable models and clear demonstrations aid learning. Distinguish the mechanisms: Classical conditioning links stimuli; operant conditioning links behaviour with consequences; observational learning involves watching others; cognitive approaches also examine expectations and understanding. These mechanisms can operate together.

questions.title: Q41. Explain the cognitive theories of learning: social cognitive theory, cognitive behavioural theory and constructivism.
questions.body: Introduction Cognitive learning views the consumer as an active problem-solver who learns through mental processes – thinking, information processing and reasoning – rather than only through reward and repetition. Three important cognitive theories are social cognitive theory, cognitive behavioural theory and constructivism. 1. Social Cognitive Theory (Albert Bandura) Learning results from the interaction of personal factors (beliefs, expectations), behaviour and environment – reciprocal determinism. 1. Self-efficacy: belief in one's ability to perform a behaviour decides whether a person tries it. 2. Observational learning from models. 3. Marketing use: tutorials, "easy to use" claims, success stories that build confidence. Example: A woman believes she can cook well with a smart kitchen appliance after watching tutorials, so she buys it. 2. Cognitive Behavioural Theory (Aaron Beck) Our thoughts (cognitions) influence our feelings and behaviour; changing thoughts can change behaviour. ```mermaid flowchart LR T["THOUGHTS"] --- F["FEELINGS"] --- B["BEHAVIOUR"] ``` 1. A thought ("I deserve a reward") creates a feeling (excitement), which leads to behaviour (an impulse purchase). 2. Reframing thoughts ("Do I need this?") reduces impulse buying. 3. Marketing / social use: campaigns that change beliefs to change behaviour (anti-smoking, saving money, healthy eating). Example: A savings app asks users "Will you still want this in a week?" before an online purchase, reducing impulse spending. 3. Constructivism (Jean Piaget, Lev Vygotsky) Learners actively construct their own knowledge by linking new information with existing knowledge and experience. 1. Piaget: learning through assimilation (fitting new information into existing ideas) and accommodation (changing ideas to fit new information). 2. Vygotsky: learning is social – it happens through interaction and guidance from others. 3. Marketing use: interactive demos, experiential marketing, product trials, online communities and comparison tools. Example: A first-time investor understands mutual funds by exploring apps, comparing them with bank FDs and discussing them with friends. 4. Supporting Ideas 1. Information processing: consumers receive information, store it in memory (sensory → short-term → long-term) and retrieve it when deciding. 2. Involvement theory: high-involvement purchases get deep processing; low-involvement purchases get little. Comparison Table | Theory | Proposed by | Key idea | Marketing use | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Social cognitive | Bandura | Person–behaviour–environment interaction; self-efficacy | Tutorials, success stories | | Cognitive behavioural | Beck | Thoughts drive feelings and behaviour | Belief-change campaigns | | Constructivism | Piaget, Vygotsky | Learners build their own knowledge | Demos, trials, communities |

questions.title: Q42. What are evaluative criteria and decision rules? Explain with examples.
questions.body: Introduction While choosing between brands, consumers compare them on certain features and then follow a rule to decide. Evaluative criteria are the product features or attributes used to compare alternatives – for example price, brand, quality, battery life and after-sales service. Decision rules (heuristics) are the procedures consumers use to choose among alternatives. 1. Compensatory Rule A weakness on one attribute can be compensated by strength on another. The brand with the highest total weighted score is chosen. Example – choosing a phone: | Attribute (weight) | Brand A | Brand B | | --- | --- | --- | | Camera (0.5) | 8 | 6 | | Battery (0.3) | 5 | 9 | | Price (0.2) | 6 | 8 | | Weighted score | 8×0.5 + 5×0.3 + 6×0.2 = 6.7 | 6×0.5 + 9×0.3 + 8×0.2 = 7.3 | Brand B is chosen (7.3 > 6.7) although Brand A has the better camera. 2. Non-Compensatory Rules A weakness cannot be made up by other strengths. 1. Conjunctive rule: set a minimum cut-off for every attribute; reject any brand below a cut-off. (Battery must be at least 6 → Brand A rejected.) 2. Disjunctive rule: set a high cut-off on one or a few key attributes; accept any brand that exceeds it. (Camera at least 8 → Brand A accepted.) 3. Lexicographic rule: rank attributes by importance and choose the brand best on the most important attribute. (Camera most important → Brand A.) 3. Affect Referral Rule Choose the brand with the best overall feeling or attitude, without detailed evaluation ("I always trust Tata"). Comparison Table | Rule | Type | How the choice is made | Result in example | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Compensatory | Compensatory | Highest weighted score | Brand B | | Conjunctive | Non-compensatory | Minimum on all attributes | Brand B | | Disjunctive | Non-compensatory | High on key attribute | Brand A | | Lexicographic | Non-compensatory | Best on most important | Brand A | | Affect referral | Simplified | Overall liking | Favourite brand | Memory aid: C-C-D-L-A – Compensatory, Conjunctive, Disjunctive, Lexicographic, Affect referral.

questions.title: Q43. Explain the Sheth model of industrial buyer behaviour.
questions.body:
Introduction In industrial buying, decisions are often made jointly by people from different departments who may disagree. The Sheth model (Jagdish Sheth, 1973) explains this joint decision making in industrial (organisational) buying through four main elements. Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart TD A["1. Psychological world of decision makers → EXPECTATIONS
background, information sources, active search,
perceptual distortion, satisfaction with past purchases"] B["2. Product- and company-specific factors → AUTONOMOUS or JOINT decision
time pressure, perceived risk, type of purchase;
orientation, size, centralisation"] C["3. Conflict resolution
problem solving, persuasion, bargaining, politicking"] D["4. Situational factors → SUPPLIER / BRAND CHOICE
strikes, recession, price changes, natural disasters"] A --> B --> C --> D ``` 1. Psychological World of the Decision Makers 1. Purchasing agents, engineers, users and others have different expectations about suppliers and brands. 2. Expectations depend on background (education, role orientation, lifestyle), information sources (salespeople, exhibitions, journals), active search, perceptual distortion and satisfaction with past purchases. 2. Factors Deciding Autonomous vs Joint Decisions 1. Product-specific factors: time pressure (urgent → autonomous), perceived risk (high → joint), type of purchase (new or capital item → joint; routine → autonomous). 2. Company-specific factors: company orientation (technology- or production-oriented), company size (large → joint), degree of centralisation (decentralised → joint decisions more likely). 3. Conflict Resolution in Joint Decisions 1. Problem solving: gathering more information and deliberating – rational. 2. Persuasion: convincing others that one's criteria fit company goals. 3. Bargaining: give-and-take ("you choose this time, I choose next time"). 4. Politicking: using power and tactics – least rational and may harm the organisation. 4. Situational Factors Unexpected events – strikes, recession, price controls, supplier problems, natural calamities – may override the planned choice. Advantages: - Recognises group decisions and conflict. - Useful for B2B selling. Limitations: - Complex and hard to measure. - Less focus on post-purchase behaviour. Comparison Table (conflict resolution methods) | Method | Nature | Rationality | | --- | --- | --- | | Problem solving | More information, discussion | Most rational | | Persuasion | Convincing others | Rational | | Bargaining | Give-and-take | Less rational | | Politicking | Power and tactics | Least rational | Example: When a factory buys a new machine, engineers prefer quality and the finance team prefers low cost; they resolve the conflict by gathering more supplier data (problem solving).

questions.title: Q44. Explain the types of communication systems: interpersonal, impersonal and persuasive communication.
questions.body: Introduction Marketers reach consumers in different ways – through a salesperson's conversation, a TV ad or a carefully designed persuasive campaign. Communication systems are classified as interpersonal, impersonal and persuasive communication. 1. Interpersonal Communication Direct, face-to-face or personal communication between two or more people. 1. Can be formal (salesperson to customer) or informal (word of mouth among friends and family). 2. Two-way, with immediate feedback; highly persuasive and trusted. 3. Examples: personal selling, word of mouth, opinion leaders, phone calls, WhatsApp recommendations. 2. Impersonal Communication Communication directed at a large, anonymous audience through mass media. 1. One-way, with delayed and indirect feedback (sales, surveys). 2. Examples: TV, radio, newspaper and magazine ads, billboards, websites, social media posts, public relations. 3. Persuasive Communication Communication intended to change attitudes or behaviour – to make consumers buy, try or prefer a brand. Factors that make communication persuasive: 1. Source credibility: expertise, trustworthiness and attractiveness of the source (doctors for toothpaste, celebrities). 2. Message structure: one-sided (only benefits – for favourable audiences) vs two-sided (benefits and limitations – more credible for educated audiences); order effects (primacy and recency); repetition. 3. Message appeals: - Rational appeal: facts, features, price, performance. - Emotional appeals: fear (insurance, road safety), humour, love, nostalgia, pride, guilt. - Comparative advertising: comparison with competitors. - Attractiveness appeal: used carefully. 4. Audience characteristics: involvement, knowledge, personality. Persuasion models: AIDA – Attention → Interest → Desire → Action; Hierarchy of effects – awareness → knowledge → liking → preference → conviction → purchase. Comparison Table | Basis | Interpersonal | Impersonal | | --- | --- | --- | | Audience | Individual or small group | Large mass audience | | Direction | Two-way | Mostly one-way | | Feedback | Immediate | Delayed | | Cost per person | High | Low | | Trust | High | Lower | | Example | Salesperson, word of mouth | TV ad, billboard | Example: A car company runs TV ads (impersonal), trains showroom staff (interpersonal) and uses a fear appeal about road safety to promote airbags (persuasive).
